title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation fraud carried out with a synthetic video call. The caller used an AI-generated likeness of a public figure to open a conversation, and the deception then ran through ordinary channels: a WhatsApp video call, a demand for processing fees, a digital payment app, and a second person claiming authority to threaten a fine. The deepfake was the entry point, not the whole scheme. The money moved because the victim believed he was dealing with a government aid process.

The failure sits at the point of contact between a member of the public and an unverified identity. Nothing in the call was checked against an official channel before payments were made. Catching it would have required the victim to verify the aid offer independently, or a platform-level signal that the video was synthetic. Neither was in place. The reporting notes this is the first deepfake case of its kind registered in the city, so there was no local precedent for the victim to recognise.

What is not established is who produced the deepfake, how it was made, or whether anyone has been identified or charged. A registered case is not a finding of guilt, and the reporting does not say the impersonated official had any involvement.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29-year-old security guard in Bengaluru named Ratikanta Giri received a WhatsApp video call on September 9 from someone using an AI-generated deepfake to pose as Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay. The caller offered him Rs 11 lakh in financial aid, then had a supposed manager demand processing fees. Giri paid over Rs 1.04 lakh through a digital payment app, including Rs 5,000, Rs 18,000, and more than Rs 50,000 after another person claiming to be a CBI officer threatened him with a fine.

Giri refused a further demand of Rs 50,000 and realized he had been cheated. He contacted the cybercrime helpline 1930 and then approached Byappanahalli police, who registered a case under the Information Technology Act. This is the first such deepfake case reported in the city. A senior officer urged people not to believe such calls or make payments based on such claims.
